arXiv:1105.1039v3 [cond-mat.stat-mech] 29 Aug 2011

Velocity fluctuations of population fronts propagating into metastable states

Baruch Meerson1, Pavel V. Sasorov2, and Yitzhak Kaplan1 Affiliation: 1Racah Institute of Physics, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem 91904, Israel Affiliation: 2Institute for Theoretical and Experimental Physics, Moscow 117218, Russia
Abstract

The position of propagating population fronts fluctuates because of the discreteness of the individuals and stochastic character of processes of birth, death and migration. Here we consider a Markov model of a population front propagating into a metastable state, and focus on the weak noise limit. For typical, small fluctuations the front motion is diffusive, and we calculate the front diffusion coefficient. We also determine the probability distribution of rare, large fluctuations of the front position and, for a given average front velocity, find the most likely population density profile of the front. Implications of the theory for population extinction risk are briefly considered.

05.40.-a, 05.10.Gg, 87.23.Cc, 02.50.Ga

I Introduction

Population fronts are ubiquitous in nature. They control the speed of a multitude of processes ranging from epidemic outbursts to invasion of species to biological evolution [1, 2]. There is a fundamental difference between fronts propagating into an unstable state and those propagating into a metastable state (a state which is linearly stable but non-linearly unstable). The former can be extremely sensitive to intrinsic noise in the leading edge [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. In particular, for pulled fronts, the front diffusion coefficient DfD_{f}, describing wandering of the front position around the position, predicted by the deterministic rate equation, is only logarithmically small with NN, the number of particles in the front region [7]. Fronts propagating into metastable states are expected to behave “normally” in this respect, and Df∼1/ND_{f}\sim 1/N scaling was conjectured [5, 6]. Surprisingly, not much is known beyond this conjecture. Yet fronts, propagating into metastable states, appear in many applications [1, 2, 8]. For example, they describe colonization and extinction waves when an Allee effect is present in the form of a critical population size needed for establishment of a local population [9, 2]. Motivated by this and other front propagation phenomena – in physics, chemistry and biology – we present here a systematic theory of fluctuations of the position of a population front propagating into a metastable state.

II Model

Let a single population of individuals (we will call them particles) reside on a one-dimensional lattice of sites labeled by index ii. The population size nin_{i} at each site varies in time as a result of two types of Markov processes [10]. The first type involves stochastic births and deaths with rates λ⁡(ni)\lambda(n_{i}) and μ⁡(ni)\mu(n_{i}), respectively. The second one is random walk of each particle between neighboring sites with rate coefficient D0D_{0}.

We assume that the typical population size scales as a large parameter, K≫1K\gg 1. Then for ni≫1n_{i}\gg 1 one can write, in the leading order [11, 12]:

λ⁡(ni)=ν​K​λ¯​(qi)andμ⁡(ni)=ν​K​μ¯​(qi),\lambda(n_{i})=\nu K\bar{\lambda}(q_{i})\;\;\;\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;\;\;\;\mu(n_{i})=\nu K\bar{\mu}(q_{i}), (1)

where qi=ni/Kq_{i}=n_{i}/K is the rescaled population size at site ii, λ¯​(qi)∼μ¯​(qi)∼1\bar{\lambda}(q_{i})\sim\bar{\mu}(q_{i})\sim 1, and ν\nu is a rate coefficient. Assuming also a fast diffusion, D0≫νD_{0}\gg\nu, we can use a continuous position coordinate xx instead of the discrete index ii. Neglecting for a moment the intrinsic noise, we arrive at a deterministic reaction-diffusion equation

∂tq=f⁡(q)+∂x2q,\partial_{t}q=f(q)+\partial_{x}^{2}q\,, (2)

where f​(q)=λ¯​(q)−μ¯​(q)f(q)=\bar{\lambda}(q)-\bar{\mu}(q), D=D0​h2D=D_{0}h^{2} is the diffusion coefficient of the random walk, and hh is the lattice constant. The position coordinate xx in Eq. (2) is rescaled by the characteristic diffusion length lD=(D/ν)1/2l_{D}=(D/\nu)^{1/2}, and time is rescaled by 1/ν1/\nu. We will restore the dimensions in our main results by recalling that the front velocity is measured in the units of ν​lD=(ν​D)1/2\nu l_{D}=(\nu D)^{1/2}, and the front diffusion coefficient DfD_{f} is measured in the units of DD.

A (deterministic) population front corresponds to a traveling wave solution (TWS) of Eq. (2), q⁡(x,t)=q⁡(ξ)q(x,t)=q(\xi), ξ=x−c0​t\xi=x-c_{0}t, which interpolates between two homogeneous states described by zeros of f⁡(q)f(q). Let one of them, q=q∗>0q=q_{*}>0, be located at x→−∞x\to-\infty, whereas the other, q=0q=0, at x→∞x\to\infty. Each of them is linearly stable: f′​(q∗)<0f^{\prime}(q_{*})<0 and f′​(0)<0f^{\prime}(0)<0. There is also a linearly unstable state quq_{u}, so that 0<qu<q∗0<q_{u}<q_{*}. The deterministic TWS q0​(ξ)q_{0}(\xi) obeys the equation

q0′′+c0​q0′+f⁡(q0)=0.q_{0}^{\prime\prime}+c_{0}q_{0}^{\prime}+f(q_{0})=0\,. (3)

This TWS is unique up to an arbitrary shift in ξ\xi. The formal definition of the metastable state in this work is based on the effective potential V⁡(q)=∫0qf⁡(q′)​d​q′V(q)=\int_{0}^{q}f(q^{\prime})\,dq^{\prime} of the deterministic problem [1, 8, 2]. The state q=q∗>0q=q_{*}>0 is advancing (c0>0c_{0}>0) when V⁡(q∗)>0V(q_{*})>0. In this case q=0q=0 is called the metastable state. For V⁡(q∗)<0V(q_{*})<0 the state q=q∗q=q_{*} is retreating (c0<0c_{0}<0), and so it is metastable. Finally, for V⁡(q∗)=0V(q_{*})=0 the front is standing, c0=0c_{0}=0, and so the two states q=q∗q=q_{*} and q=0q=0 coexist. The typical front width is on the order of lDl_{D}.

Now we go back to the discrete-lattice model and describe stochastic dynamics of the population. Introduce the multivariate probability distribution P⁡(𝐧,t)=P⁡(n1,n2,…,t)=P⁡(𝐧^,ni,t)P(\mathbf{n},t)=P(n_{1},n_{2},\dots,t)=P(\hat{\mathbf{n}},n_{i},t), where i=1,2,…i=1,2,\dots and 𝐧^\hat{\mathbf{n}} denotes the vector of all nn’s not explicitly written, see e.g. Ref. [10]. For the continuous-time Markov processes of on-site births and deaths and unbiased random walk between neighboring sites, the master equation for P⁡(𝐧,t)P(\mathbf{n},t) has the following form:

∂tP⁡(𝐧,t)\displaystyle\partial_{t}P(\mathbf{n},t) =\displaystyle= ∑i{λ⁡(ni−1)​P​(𝐧^,ni−1,t)+μ⁡(ni+1)​P​(𝐧^,ni+1,t)−[λ⁡(ni)+μ⁡(ni)]​P​(𝐧,t)}\displaystyle\sum_{i}\Big\{\lambda(n_{i}-1)P(\hat{\mathbf{n}},n_{i}-1,t)+\mu(n_{i}+1)P(\hat{\mathbf{n}},n_{i}+1,t)-[\lambda(n_{i})+\mu(n_{i})]P(\mathbf{n},t)\Big\} (4)
+\displaystyle+ D0​∑i{(ni−1+1)​P​(𝐧^,ni−1+1,ni−1,t)+(ni+1+1)​P​(𝐧^,ni−1,ni+1+1,t)−2​ni​P​(𝐧,t)},\displaystyle D_{0}\sum_{i}\Big\{(n_{i-1}+1)P(\hat{\mathbf{n}},n_{i-1}+1,n_{i}-1,t)+(n_{i+1}+1)P(\hat{\mathbf{n}},n_{i}-1,n_{i+1}+1,t)-2n_{i}P(\mathbf{n},t)\Big\}\,,

where we have returned to dimensional units.

III Small fluctuations

Small fluctuations around the deterministic TWS can be described by the (approximate) Fokker-Planck equation obtained, via a truncated expansion, from Eq. (4), see e.g. Ref. [13]:

∂tP⁡(𝐪,t)\displaystyle\partial_{t}P(\mathbf{q},t) =\displaystyle= −ν∑i∂∂qi{f(qi)P−12​K∂∂qi[g(qi)P]}\displaystyle-\nu\sum\limits_{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{i}}\,\left\{f(q_{i})\,P-\frac{1}{2K}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{i}}\,\left[g(q_{i})\,P\right]\right\} (5)
+\displaystyle+ D0∑i(∂∂qi−∂∂qi+1)[(qi−qi+1)P\displaystyle D_{0}\sum\limits_{i}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{i}}-\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{i+1}}\right)\bigg[\left(q_{i}-q_{i+1}\right)\,P\bigg.
+\displaystyle+ qi+qi+12​K(∂∂qi−∂∂qi+1)P].\displaystyle\left.\frac{q_{i}+q_{i+1}}{2K}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{i}}-\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{i+1}}\right)\,P\right]\,.

Here g​(q)=λ¯​(q)+μ¯​(q)g(q)=\bar{\lambda}(q)+\bar{\mu}(q) is a rescaled on-site diffusion coefficient in the space of population sizes. Instead of dealing with the Fokker-Planck equation directly, we will consider the Langevin equation to which it is equivalent. Reintroducing a continuous description in space, we obtain [14]

∂tq⁡(x,t)\displaystyle\partial_{t}q(x,t) =\displaystyle= ν​f​(q)+D​∂x2q+ν​g​(q)​hK​η​(x,t)\displaystyle\nu f(q)+D\partial_{x}^{2}q+\sqrt{\frac{\nu g(q)\,h}{K}}\,\eta(x,t) (6)
+\displaystyle+ ∂x[2​q​(x,t)​D​hK​χ​(x,t)],\displaystyle\partial_{x}\left[\sqrt{\frac{2q(x,t)\,Dh}{K}}\,\chi(x,t)\right]\,,

where η⁡(x,t)\eta(x,t) and χ⁡(x,t)\chi(x,t) are independent Gaussian noises which have zero means and are delta-correlated both in xx and in tt:

⟨η⁡(x,t)​η​(x′,t′)⟩=⟨χ⁡(x,t)​χ​(x′,t′)⟩=δ⁡(x−x′)​δ​(t−t′).\left\langle\eta(x,t)\eta(x^{\prime},t^{\prime})\right\rangle=\left\langle\chi(x,t)\chi(x^{\prime},t^{\prime})\right\rangle=\delta(x-x^{\prime})\,\delta(t-t^{\prime}). (7)

The first two terms on the right hand side of Eq. (6) are the same terms as in the deterministic equation (2). The last two terms describe multiplicative noises coming from the on-site birth and death processes (the third term), and from the random walk (the fourth term, which has the form of a flux). Importantly, the magnitudes of the two noise terms are comparable to each other in the front region. The flux term does not appear in the Langevin equations used in many papers for modeling fluctuations of the front position caused by external noise [15, 16]. In addition, for external noise the analogs of function g⁡(q)g(q) are chosen ad hoc [15, 16], whereas g⁡(q)g(q) in Eq. (6) is uniquely determined by the on-site birth and death rates.

Pechenik and Levine [17] used the Doi-Peliti formalism [18] to derive the Langevin equation for a microscopic model which includes processes A⇄2​AA\rightleftarrows 2A and random walk. This model corresponds to propagation into unstable state. However, the derivation would hold for propagation into a metastable state as well. The Langevin equation of Ref. [17] describes the evolution of the system in terms of the dynamics of a sequence of Poissonian states [10]. A possible advantage of their description is that the random walk noise is “absorbed” by the variables and does not appear explicitly. An advantage of Eq. (6) is that it provides a direct description of the dynamics of the system in terms of the (rescaled) population size q⁡(x,t)q(x,t).

Rescaling the position coordinate xx and time tt by lDl_{D} and 1/ν1/\nu, respectively, we can rewrite Eq. (6) as

∂tq(x,t)=f(q)+∂x2q(x,t)+N−1/2R(x,t,q),\partial_{t}q(x,t)=f(q)+\partial_{x}^{2}q(x,t)+N^{-1/2}R(x,t,q)\,, (8)

where

R⁡(x,t,q)=g⁡(q)​η​(x,t)+∂x[2​q​χ​(x,t)],R(x,t,q)=\sqrt{g(q)}\,\eta(x,t)+\partial_{x}[\sqrt{2q}\,\chi(x,t)]\,, (9)

where N=K​lD/h≫1N=Kl_{D}/h\gg 1 is the typical number of particles in the front region. The smallness of N−1/2N^{-1/2}, the effective magnitude of the intrinsic noise, enables one to solve Eq. (8) perturbatively around the deterministic TWS, see Refs. [15, 16]. One looks for a perturbative solution

q⁡(ξX,t)=q0​(ξX)+q1​(ξX,t),|q1|≪q0,q(\xi_{X},t)=q_{0}(\xi_{X})+q_{1}(\xi_{X},t)\,,\;\;\;|q_{1}|\ll q_{0}\,, (10)

where ξX=x−c0​t−X⁡(t)\xi_{X}=x-c_{0}t-X(t), and X⁡(t)X(t) describes the noise-driven displacement of the front position with respect to the deterministic TWS. Going over to the variables ξX\xi_{X} and tt and linearizing Eq. (8) around q0q_{0}, we obtain

∂tq1=ℒ^q1+X˙q0′+N−1/2R(x,t,q0),\partial_{t}q_{1}=\hat{{\cal L}}q_{1}+\dot{X}q_{0}^{\prime}+N^{-1/2}R(x,t,q_{0})\,, (11)

where

ℒ^=∂ξ2+c0∂ξ+f′(q0),\hat{\cal L}=\partial^{2}_{\xi}+c_{0}\partial_{\xi}+f^{\prime}(q_{0})\,, (12)

and we kept the old variable xx in the noise term.

X˙​(t)\dot{X}(t) can be found from the solvability condition of Eq. (11). To this end let us consider the eigenmodes of the operator ℒ^\hat{\cal L}: ℒ^​ϕn=an​ϕn\hat{\cal L}\phi_{n}=a_{n}\phi_{n}. The zero mode ϕ0​(ξ)=q0′​(ξ)\phi_{0}(\xi)=q_{0}^{\prime}(\xi), for which a0=0a_{0}=0, is the Goldstone mode, coming from the translational invariance of the deterministic TWS. Importantly, the lowest excited mode is gapped [15, 19]. We expand

q1​(ξX,t)=∑nbn​(t)​ϕn​(ξX),q_{1}(\xi_{X},t)=\sum_{n}{b_{n}(t)\phi_{n}(\xi_{X})}\,,

and fix the definition of X⁡(t)X(t) by setting b0​(t)=0b_{0}(t)=0. Now we multiply Eq. (11) by ec0​ξ​ϕ0​(ξ)e^{c_{0}\xi}\phi_{0}(\xi) and integrate over ξ\xi from −∞-\infty to ∞\infty. As the operator ec0​ξ​ℒ^e^{c_{0}\xi}\hat{\cal L} is Hermitian, the functions ϕn\phi_{n} with different nn are orthogonal to each other with weight function ec0​ξe^{c_{0}\xi}, so upon normalization

∫−∞∞d​ξ​ϕn​(ξ)​ϕm​(ξ)​ec0​ξ=δn​m,\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\xi\phi_{n}(\xi)\phi_{m}(\xi)e^{c_{0}\xi}=\delta_{nm}\,, (13)

where δn​m\delta_{nm} is the Kronecker’s delta. As a result,

X˙=−∫−∞∞d​ξ​q0′​ec0​ξ​R​(x,t,q0)N1/2​∫−∞∞d​ξ​(q0′)2​ec0​ξ.\dot{X}=-\frac{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\xi\,q_{0}^{\prime}\,e^{c_{0}\xi}R(x,t,q_{0})}{N^{1/2}\,\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\xi\,(q_{0}^{\prime})^{2}\,e^{c_{0}\xi}}\,. (14)

The front diffusion coefficient DfD_{f}, in the frame moving with the velocity c0c_{0}, is given by the relation

Df=limt→∞∫0td​t1​∫0td​t2​⟨X˙​(t1)​X˙​(t2)⟩2​t.D_{f}=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\int_{0}^{t}dt_{1}\int_{0}^{t}dt_{2}\,\langle\dot{X}(t_{1})\dot{X}(t_{2})\rangle}{2t}\,. (15)

Using Eqs. (15), (14) and (9) we obtain, after some algebra (see Appendix),

Df=Ds0​N,D_{f}=\frac{D}{s_{0}N}\,, (16)

where

s0=[∫−∞∞d​ξ​(q0′)2​ec0​ξ]2∫−∞∞d​ξ​{12​(q0′​ec0​ξ)2​g​(q0)+q0​[(q0′​ec0​ξ)′]2}.s_{0}=\frac{\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\xi(q_{0}^{\prime})^{2}e^{c_{0}\xi}\right]^{2}}{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\xi\,\Big\{\frac{1}{2}\,(q_{0}^{\prime}e^{c_{0}\xi})^{2}\,g(q_{0})+q_{0}\left[\left(q_{0}^{\prime}e^{c_{0}\xi}\right)^{\prime}\right]^{2}\Big\}}\,. (17)

That is, in order to calculate the front diffusion coefficient one only needs two ingredients: the deterministic TWS q0​(ξ)q_{0}(\xi) and the function g​(q)=λ¯​(q)+μ¯​(q)g(q)=\bar{\lambda}(q)+\bar{\mu}(q) evaluated on q0​(ξ)q_{0}(\xi). As expected [5, 6], Df/DD_{f}/D scales as N−1N^{-1}, in stark contrast with the propagation into an unstable state where Df/D∼(ln⁡N)−3D_{f}/D\sim(\ln N)^{-3} [7]. The first and second terms in the denominator of Eq. (17) come from the birth-death noise and random walk noise, respectively. We note that the numerator and the first term in the denominator appeared in the calculations of the front diffusion coefficient for the case of external fluctuations [15, 16]. In that case, however, g⁡(q)g(q) is unrelated to the on-site birth and death rates. Importantly, for f′​(q∗)<0f^{\prime}(q_{*})<0 and f′​(0)<0f^{\prime}(0)<0, all the integrals entering Eq. (17) converge.

IV Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (WKB) approximation

Large fluctuations of the front position render the Fokker-Planck approximation (5) and the ensuing Langevin equation (6) inapplicable. However, one can still exploit the small parameter 1/N1/N via a WKB approximation, see e.g. [13, 20, 21], by making the ansatz P⁡(𝐧,t)=exp⁡[−K​S​(𝐪,t)]P(\mathbf{n},t)=\exp[-KS(\mathbf{q},t)] in the master equation (4). In the leading order in 1/K1/K, this brings about a Hamilton-Jacobi equation ∂tS+H⁡(𝐪,∂𝐪S)=0\partial_{t}S+H(\mathbf{q},\partial_{\mathbf{q}}S)=0. In the continuum limit in xx, the Hamiltonian functional H=ν​∫d​x​wH=\nu\int dx\,w. Here

w=H0​(q,p)−∂xq​∂xp+q​(∂xp)2w=H_{0}(q,p)-\partial_{x}q\,\partial_{x}p+q\left(\partial_{x}p\right)^{2} (18)

is the rescaled Hamiltonian density, xx is rescaled by lDl_{D}, and

H0​(q,p)=λ¯​(q)​(ep−1)+μ¯​(q)​(e−p−1)H_{0}(q,p)=\bar{\lambda}(q)\left(e^{p}-1\right)+\bar{\mu}(q)\left(e^{-p}-1\right) (19)

is the rescaled on-site Hamiltonian [13, 20]. The last term in Eq. (18) comes from the random walk noise. Note the identities H0​(q,0)=0H_{0}(q,0)=0, ∂pH0​(q,0)=f⁡(q)\partial_{p}H_{0}(q,0)=f(q), ∂q​pH0​(q,0)=f′​(q)\partial_{qp}H_{0}(q,0)=f^{\prime}(q) and ∂p​pH0​(q,0)=g⁡(q)\partial_{pp}H_{0}(q,0)=g(q).

Instead of directly solving the Hamilton-Jacobi equation for S⁡(𝐪,t)S(\mathbf{q},t), consider the Hamilton’s equations of motion

∂tq\displaystyle\partial_{t}q =\displaystyle= ∂pH0​(q,p)+∂x2q−2​∂x(q​∂xp),\displaystyle\partial_{p}H_{0}(q,p)+\partial_{x}^{2}q-2\partial_{x}\left(q\partial_{x}p\right), (20)
∂tp\displaystyle\partial_{t}p =\displaystyle= −∂qH0(q,p)−∂x2p−(∂xp)2\displaystyle-\partial_{q}H_{0}(q,p)-\partial_{x}^{2}p-\left(\partial_{x}p\right)^{2} (21)

for the population size q⁡(x,t)q(x,t) and effective momentum p⁡(x,t)=h​δ​S/δ​qp(x,t)=h\,\delta S/\delta q. Deterministic dynamics take place in the invariant hyperplane p=0p=0, where Eq. (20) reduces to Eq. (2). Fluctuations involve a non-zero p⁡(x,t)p(x,t), and this is the case of our interest. To have a well-defined problem for Eqs. (20) and (21) one needs to specify the boundary conditions, both in space and in time. The boundary conditions in space correspond to zero-energy fixed points of the on-site Hamiltonian: {q⁡(−∞,t),p⁡(−∞,t)}={q∗,0}\{q(-\infty,t),p(-\infty,t)\}=\{q_{*},0\} and {q⁡(∞,t),p⁡(∞,t)}={0,0}\{q(\infty,t),p(\infty,t)\}=\{0,0\}. The boundary conditions in time involve, in general, specifying kink-like population size profiles q1​(x)q_{1}(x) and q2​(x)q_{2}(x) at t=0t=0 and t=τt=\tau, respectively. After having solved the Hamilton’s equations, one can calculate the action along the trajectory of the system in the functional phase space q,pq,p:

K​𝒮=N​∫−∞∞d​x​∫0ν​τd​t​[p⁡(x,t)​∂tq−w].K\mathcal{S}=N\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\int_{0}^{\nu\tau}dt\;[p(x,t)\partial_{t}q-w]\,. (22)

We are interested in the probability of observing, in the frame moving with the velocity c0c_{0}, a front displacement XX during a time interval which is much longer than the front relaxation time: ν​τ≫1\nu\tau\gg 1. Our crucial assumption is that this probability is described, in the leading order of 1/(ν​τ)≪11/(\nu\tau)\ll 1, by a traveling wave solution (TWS) of Eqs. (20) and (21). This leads to two coupled ordinary differential equations for q⁡(ξ)q(\xi) and p⁡(ξ)p(\xi), where ξ=x−c​t\xi=x-ct and c=X/τc=X/\tau is the average front velocity during time τ\tau:

q′′−2​(q​p′)′+c​q′+∂pH0​(q,p)\displaystyle q^{\prime\prime}-2(qp^{\prime})^{\prime}+cq^{\prime}+\partial_{p}H_{0}(q,p) =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0\,, (23)
p′′+(p′)2−c​p′+∂qH0​(q,p)\displaystyle p^{\prime\prime}+(p^{\prime})^{2}-cp^{\prime}+\partial_{q}H_{0}(q,p) =\displaystyle= 0.\displaystyle 0\,. (24)

The boundary conditions are q⁡(−∞)=q∗q(-\infty)=q_{*} and q⁡(∞)=p⁡(−∞)=p⁡(∞)=0q(\infty)=p(-\infty)=p(\infty)=0. As ∂tq=−c​q′​(ξ)\partial_{t}q=-cq^{\prime}(\xi) for a TWS, Eq. (22) reduces to

K𝒮(c)=−Nντ∫−∞∞dξ[cp(ξ)q′(ξ)+w].K\mathcal{S}(c)=-N\nu\tau\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\xi\;[cp(\xi)q^{\prime}(\xi)+w]\,. (25)

Remarkably, Eqs. (23) and (24) possess a conservation law:

H0​[q⁡(ξ),p⁡(ξ)]+q′​p′−q​(p′)2=C=constH_{0}[q(\xi),p(\xi)]+q^{\prime}p^{\prime}-q(p^{\prime})^{2}=C=\mbox{const} (26)

where, by virtue of the boundary conditions, C=0C=0.

Although especially suitable for dealing with large fluctuations of the front position, the WKB theory also captures typical, small fluctuations. To see it, let us linearize Eqs. (23) and (24) around the deterministic TWS (3):

q⁡(ξ)=q0​(ξ)+u⁡(ξ)​and​c=c0+δ​c,q(\xi)=q_{0}(\xi)+u(\xi)\;\;\;\mbox{and}\;\;\;c=c_{0}+\delta c\,, (27)

where |u|∼|p|∼|δ​c|≪1|u|\sim|p|\sim|\delta c|\ll 1. We obtain

ℒ^​u\displaystyle\hat{\cal L}u =\displaystyle= −δ​c​q0′−g⁡(q0)​p+2​(q0​p′)′,\displaystyle-\delta c\,q_{0}^{\prime}-g(q_{0})p+2(q_{0}p^{\prime})^{\prime}\,, (28)
ℒ^∗​p\displaystyle\hat{\cal L}^{*}p =\displaystyle= 0\displaystyle 0 (29)

with zero boundary conditions at ±∞\pm\infty. The operator ℒ^\hat{\cal L} was defined in Eq. (12), whereas the operator ℒ^∗=dξ2−c0​dξ+f′​(q0)\hat{\cal L}^{*}=d^{2}_{\xi}-c_{0}d_{\xi}+f^{\prime}(q_{0}) is adjoint to ℒ^\hat{\cal L}.

For the small deviations, the action (25) can be expanded to second order. The linear terms cancel out, whereas the quadratic terms yield, after some algebra,

K​𝒮​(δ​c)=N​ν​τ​∫−∞∞d​ξ​[12​g​(q0)​p2+q0​(p′)2].K\mathcal{S}(\delta c)=N\nu\tau\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\xi\left[\frac{1}{2}g(q_{0})p^{2}+q_{0}(p^{\prime})^{2}\right]\,. (30)

As one can see, the knowledge of p⁡(ξ)p(\xi) alone is sufficient for evaluating the action (and the front diffusion coefficient, see below) for small fluctuations. Therefore, let us consider Eq. (29). One independent solution of this equation, p1​(ξ)=ec0​ξ​q0′​(ξ)p_{1}(\xi)=e^{c_{0}\xi}q_{0}^{\prime}(\xi), obeys the zero boundary conditions at ±∞\pm\infty [22]. Therefore, p⁡(ξ)=p0​p1​(ξ)p(\xi)=p_{0}p_{1}(\xi) with an a priori unknown constant p0p_{0}. To determine this constant, we turn to Eq. (28) for u⁡(ξ)u(\xi), where p⁡(ξ)p(\xi) enters the effective forcing term

F⁡(ξ)=−δ​c​q0′​(ξ)−p0​g​[q0​(ξ)]​p1​(ξ)+2​p0​[q0​(ξ)​p1′​(ξ)]′.F(\xi)=-\delta c\,q_{0}^{\prime}(\xi)-p_{0}g[q_{0}(\xi)]p_{1}(\xi)+2p_{0}[q_{0}(\xi)p_{1}^{\prime}(\xi)]^{\prime}\,.

Demanding zero boundary conditions at ±∞\pm\infty, one can obtain a solvability condition: ∫−∞∞d​ξ​ec0​ξ​q0′​(ξ)​F​(ξ)=0\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\xi\,e^{c_{0}\xi}q_{0}^{\prime}(\xi)F(\xi)=0. This yields

p0δ​c=−∫−∞∞d​ξ​(q0′)2​ec0​ξ∫−∞∞d​ξ​{(q0′​ec0​ξ)2​g​(q0)+2​q0​[(ec0​ξ​q0′)′]2}.\frac{p_{0}}{\delta c}=-\,\frac{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\xi(q_{0}^{\prime})^{2}\,e^{c_{0}\xi}}{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\xi\big\{(q_{0}^{\prime}e^{c_{0}\xi})^{2}g(q_{0})+2q_{0}\left[(e^{c_{0}\xi}q_{0}^{\prime})^{\prime}\right]^{2}\big\}}\,. (31)

Then, from Eq. (30), K​𝒮=(1/4)​s0​N​ν​τ​(δ​c)2K\mathcal{S}=(1/4)s_{0}N\nu\tau(\delta c)^{2}, where s0s_{0} is defined in Eq. (17), and δ​c\delta c is still dimensionless. Recalling that δ​c=X/τ−c0\delta c=X/\tau-c_{0}, we see that the probability distribution P⁡(X,τ)P(X,\tau) is a Gaussian in the frame moving with the deterministic front velocity c0c_{0}. Normalizing this distribution to unity we obtain, already in the dimensional variables,

P⁡(X,τ)≃(s0​N4​π​D​τ)1/2​exp⁡(−s0​N​X24​D​τ),P(X,\tau)\simeq\left(\frac{s_{0}N}{4\pi D\tau}\right)^{1/2}\exp\left(-\frac{s_{0}NX^{2}}{4D\tau}\right)\,, (32)

where |X/τ−c0|≪(ν​D)1/2|X/\tau-c_{0}|\ll(\nu D)^{1/2}. Equation (32) coincides with the Green function of a diffusion equation, so the front diffusion coefficient Df=D/(s0​N)D_{f}=D/(s_{0}N), in a perfect agreement with Eq. (16), derived from the Langevin equation.

Rare large fluctuations of the front position correspond to |p|≳1|p|\gtrsim 1 in the WKB formalism. This demands a full nonlinear solution of Eqs. (23) and (24) which in general is only accessible numerically. Examples of such calculations are presented in the next section.

We should emphasize that our results on fluctuating extinction fronts are conditional on the absence of attempted extinction events in the region to the left of the front. This conditioning is especially important for c0<0c_{0}<0. Here an extinction front appears already in deterministic description, and formation of critical nuclei of the state q=0q=0 is possible [8, 13].

V Example

Consider three on-site reactions: A→0A\to 0, 2​A→3​A2A\to 3A and 3​A→2​A3A\to 2A, with rate coefficients μ0\mu_{0}, λ0\lambda_{0} and σ0\sigma_{0}, respectively  [12, 13, 23, 24]. It is convenient to perform the rescaling so that λ¯​(q)=2​q2\bar{\lambda}(q)=2q^{2} and μ¯​(q)=γ​q+q3\bar{\mu}(q)=\gamma\,q+q^{3}, where ν=3​λ02/(8​σ0)\nu=3\lambda_{0}^{2}/(8\sigma_{0}), K=3​λ0/(2​σ0)K=3\lambda_{0}/(2\sigma_{0}), and γ=8​μ0​σ0/(3​λ02)\gamma=8\mu_{0}\sigma_{0}/(3\lambda_{0}^{2}). The on-site dynamics exhibits bistability at δ2≡1−γ>0\delta^{2}\equiv 1-\gamma>0. In this case the zeros of function f⁡(q)=−q⁡(q−qu)​(q−q∗)f(q)=-q\,(q-q_{u})(q-q_{*}) describe two stable fixed points of deterministic theory, 00 and q∗=1+δq_{*}=1+\delta, and an unstable fixed point qu=1−δq_{u}=1-\delta such that 0<qu<q∗0<q_{u}<q_{*}. The deterministic TWS q0​(x−c0​t)q_{0}(x-c_{0}t) is [1, 8, 2]

q0​(ξ)=δ+11+e(1+δ)​ξ/2,c0=3​δ−12,q_{0}(\xi)=\frac{\delta+1}{1+e^{(1+\delta)\,\xi/\sqrt{2}}}\,,\;\;\;\;c_{0}=\frac{3\delta-1}{\sqrt{2}}\,, (33)

so the deterministic front is advancing at 1/3<δ<11/3<\delta<1, retreating at 0<δ<1/30<\delta<1/3 and stationary at δ=1/3\delta=1/3. The function g⁡(q)=λ¯​(q)+μ¯​(q)=γ​q+2​q2+q3g(q)=\bar{\lambda}(q)+\bar{\mu}(q)=\gamma\,q+2q^{2}+q^{3}.

V.1 Small fluctuations

Within theory of small fluctuations, one only needs to calculate s0=s0​(δ)s_{0}=s_{0}(\delta) from Eq. (17) which enters the front diffusion coefficient Df=D/(s0​N)D_{f}=D/(s_{0}N). All the integrals can be evaluated analytically. The result is a bit cumbersome, however, so we only present it graphically, see Fig. 1, and give its asymptotes:

s0​(δ)={2​2​δ9+178​2​δ2135,0<δ≪1,5​26−95​2​(1−δ)72,0<1−δ≪1 .s_{0}(\delta)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{2\sqrt{2}\,\delta}{9}+\frac{178\sqrt{2}\,\delta^{2}}{135}\,,&\mbox{$0<\delta\ll 1$}\,,\\ \\ \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{6}-\frac{95\sqrt{2}\,(1-\delta)}{72}\,,&\mbox{$0<1-\delta\ll 1$\,.}\end{array}\right. (34)

The latter asymptote corresponds to μ0​σ0≪λ02\mu_{0}\sigma_{0}\ll\lambda_{0}^{2}. For δ=1/3\delta=1/3 (when the deterministic front is stationary) we obtain s0=2/6s_{0}=\sqrt{2}/6.

As one can see from Fig. 1, the front diffusion Df=D/(s​N)D_{f}=D/(sN) for the extinction fronts is stronger than for the colonization fronts. Furthermore, DfD_{f} diverges as 1/δ1/\delta when δ→0\delta\to 0. This happens because, in this case, the integral in the denominator of Eq. (17) diverges at ξ=−∞\xi=-\infty. The divergence comes from the first term of the integrand, describing the birth-death noise. Notice that δ=0\delta=0 is the (saddle-node) bifurcation point of this model, and it is hardly surprising that fluctuations are enhanced in the vicinity of this bifurcation. Actually, very close to the bifurcation point our perturbation theory breaks down. Indeed, it is only valid when the typical value of X˙\dot{X} is much less than the deterministic front velocity ∼(ν​D)1/2\sim(\nu D)^{1/2}. By virtue of Eqs. (14) and (9), this boils down to a strong inequality N​δ≫1N\delta\gg 1.

On the other hand, DfD_{f} behaves regularly at δ=1\delta=1, that is when the reaction A→0A\to 0 is absent. Here s0s_{0} takes its maximum value 5​2/65\sqrt{2}/6, so DfD_{f} reaches its minimum for this model. Notice that, for the reactions 2​A⇄3​A2A\rightleftarrows 3A the state q=0q=0 is marginally stable, but unstable with respect to any finite perturbation q>0q>0.

V.2 Large fluctuations

Now consider large deviations of the front position. We solved nonlinear equations (23) and (24) for the TWS by the shooting method [25]. For given δ\delta and cc we first establish analytically, by linearization, the asymptotic behavior of the solutions at large negative ξ\xi, where |q−q∗|≪1|q-q_{*}|\ll 1 and |p|≪1|p|\ll 1. This leaves us with two arbitrary constants instead of four. By fixing one of them, we fix the location of the solution in ξ\xi, and are therefore left with a single shooting parameter. The conservation law (26) is used for accuracy control.

Figure 2 which shows the numerically found q⁡(ξ)q(\xi) profile for δ=1/3\delta=1/3 and c=2​2/3c=2\sqrt{2}/3 (a) and c=−2/3c=-\sqrt{2}/3 (b). Recall that the deterministic front is stationary in this case, so such high front velocities demand large fluctuations. The q⁡(ξ)q(\xi) profile – the most probable population size profile for this front velocity – is steeper than the deterministic profile in Fig. 2a, and less steep that the deterministic profile in Fig. 2b.

Figure 3 shows the numerically found rescaled “action accumulation rate”

d​sd​t=−∫dξ(cpq′+w)\frac{ds}{dt}=-\int d\xi(cpq^{\prime}+w) (35)

[see Eq. (25)] versus cc for δ=1/3\delta=1/3. For small |c||c| the numerical results agree with the linear theory prediction d​s/d​t=2​(δ​c)2/24ds/dt=\sqrt{2}\,(\delta c)^{2}/24. The tails of the distribution ∼exp[−K𝒮(c)]=exp(−Nντds/dt)\sim\exp[-K\mathcal{S}(c)]=\exp(-N\nu\tau ds/dt), however, are strongly non-Gaussian: under-populated for fluctuations pushing the front to the right (toward colonization), and over-populated for fluctuations pushing the front to the left (toward population extinction). That is, there is a much higher probability, at c0=0c_{0}=0, to observe an unusually fast extinction front, than an unusually fast colonization front. This feature, however, can be model-dependent.

VI Implications for Population Extinction

Now let the spatial system size be large but finite: L≫lDL\gg l_{D}, with impenetrable (reflecting) boundaries at x=0x=0 and x=Lx=L. We still assume bistability, with q=q∗q=q_{*} and q=0q=0 being two linearly stable fixed points of the deterministic description. The zero population size throughout the system is an absorbing state of the stochastic dynamics and, in the absence of immigration, the population ultimately reaches this state with probability one.

Let at t=0t=0 a population front be located at x=x0x=x_{0}, where 0<x0<L0<x_{0}<L and not too close to the boundaries. As before, we assume that the populated state q=q∗q=q_{*} is on the left. The mean time to extinction, T¯\bar{T} can be very different depending on whether the deterministic front is retreating, c0<0c_{0}<0, or advancing, c0>0c_{0}>0. For c0<0c_{0}<0, the population goes extinct essentially deterministically, and T¯≃x0/|c0|\bar{T}\simeq x_{0}/|c_{0}| scales as the system size LL. For c0>0c_{0}>0 the front first populates the whole system, around q=q∗q=q_{*}, with probability close to 1. This happens on a time scale (L−x0)/c0(L-x_{0})/c_{0}. Then the probability that the population goes extinct by time tt grows with tt very slowly, as T¯\bar{T} is expected to be exponentially long [13, 20].

Now, what happens in the special case of c0=0c_{0}=0 [26]? Here the front position wanders because of the intrinsic noise. As a result, there are two routes to extinction. In the first route the wandering front first reaches the left boundary x=0x=0 where the population gets extinct rapidly. In the second route, the front first reaches x=Lx=L. Here the population develops a long-lived quasi-stationary distribution around q=q∗q=q_{*}, and the probability to go extinct by time tt grows with time very slowly [13, 20].

The probabilities plp_{l} and prp_{r} of each of the two routes to occur, and the corresponding conditional mean times to extinction T¯l\bar{T}_{l} and T¯r\bar{T}_{r} are described, in the leading order, by a classical first passage problem for random walk (of the front) in an interval [10, 27]. Therefore, we immediately obtain pl=1−x0/Lp_{l}=1-x_{0}/L and pr=x0/Lp_{r}=x_{0}/L. For the extinction via the left boundary, T¯l\bar{T}_{l} coincides, in the leading order, with the average first-passage time. The latter,

Tl¯≃L​x0Df​(2−x0L),\bar{T_{l}}\simeq\frac{Lx_{0}}{D_{f}}\left(2-\frac{x_{0}}{L}\right)\,, (36)

is well known, see e.g. Ref. [27], p. 47. Typically, Tl¯∼L2/Df\bar{T_{l}}\sim L^{2}/D_{f} in this case. For the extinction via the right boundary, the conditional mean time to extinction T¯r\bar{T}_{r} is expected to be exponentially long: much longer than the first-passage time for that boundary.

VII Summary

We have developed a systematic theory of velocity fluctuations of a population front propagating into a metastable state. These fluctuations result from the intrinsic noises of reactions (births, deaths, etc.) and random walk, and we have identified the contributions of each of these noises to the velocity fluctuations. For typical, small fluctuations we have derived, from the underlying microscopic model, the Fokker-Planck equation and the effective Langevin equation. We have calculated the front diffusion coefficient using two different methods. The first method involved a perturbative solution of the Langevin equation in the weak-noise-limit, 1/N≪11/N\ll 1. The second method employed a perturbative solution of WKB equations in the form of a traveling front which involves both the rescaled population size q⁡(x,t)q(x,t) and the effective momentum p⁡(x,t)p(x,t). As expected, the front diffusion coefficient scales with NN as 1/N1/N. We have also evaluated, with a WKB theory, the probability of rare large fluctuations of the front. Here the probability distribution of the front position, in the frame moving with the deterministic front velocity, turns out to be non-Gaussian and strongly asymmetric. We have also considered some implications of the theory for evaluating the population extinction risk. Our approach is readily extendable to multiple-step on-site processes such as n​A→(n+k)​AnA\to(n+k)A, where nn and kk are integers, and kk is not too large [20, 23]. Finally, most of our results (one notable exception being the extinction aspects considered in Sec. VI) remain valid when both of the two linearly stable fixed points of f⁡(q)f(q) describe populated states, as in the spruce budworm model, see e.g. Ref. [1], p. 7.

It would be natural to expect that |c¯−c0|∼N−α|\bar{c}-c_{0}|\sim N^{-\alpha}, where α≥1\alpha\geq 1 [6, 28]. However, it has been argued recently [29] that |c¯−c0||\bar{c}-c_{0}| can be exponentially small in NN.
  • [27] S. Redner, A Guide to First-Passage Processes (Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, UK, 2001).
  • [28] D. A. Kessler, Z. Ner, and L.M. Sander, Phys. Rev. E 58, 107 (1998).
  • [29] E. Khain, Y. T. Lin, and L. M. Sander, Europhys. Letters 93, 28001 (2011).
